title: Legends of Runeterra Clone Process, or: How to save games from the game industry.
author: matthewjosephtaylor
selftext:
Having a lot of luck recently with starting with a straight clone of a game I like and want to play as a jumping off point.  
  
Sadly LoR got zombified a few years back (not quite dead or alive). The goal here is to get myself access to a game I want to play that the original creator semi-abandoned.

If/when I ever decide to release the game I'll rip out the artwork/IP (I have no desire to get sued). But for me playing around it is quite helpful to re-use the art/cards/etc directly to get to the fun fast.

I view this technique similar to 'copying from the old masters'. Our AI pals love having examples to work from. So the first step is to create a faithful copy. Call it an 'advanced prototyping' stage. Well known technique, this isn't even innovative, just a lot easier.

This technique gets one to an actual playable fun game \*quickly\* without getting stuck in the weeds. The weeds are motivation killers and I'm sure we all have endless folders of games that fell prey to lack of motivation.

I think that in future this will just be how gamedev is done: have AI clone/remix existing games that one has interest in to use as mechanism for selecting the 'good parts' from the game(s). 

The "Hello World" and base skeleton of the project will start from a living breathing fun game not a blank canvas. And maybe it goes no further. I expect most people will 'scratch their own itch' going forward, and play other peoples games largely for inspiration or challenge of playing within an artificial constraint.

I think we are now in the era of bespoke custom 1-player games where 1-player means the entire game is largely designed/created for/by the player. JIT gaming? :)

Call it distilling or cloning or copying or theft or learning. It is the same process mankind has used for forever to advance the arts. Now it is just that any sufficiently motivated individual can do it, better, faster, stronger.

Sharing here to see if there might be others like myself are doing similar process. Think there are a lot of tricks to capturing the existing catalog of games, maybe enough for a community to form or at least an interesting discussion thread.

Perhaps the purpose of gamedev itself becomes more focused on creating the game(s) one wants to play and actually \*playing games\*. IMHO now is the best time to get started in the game of gamedev. :)
